_comment: The report's cumulative section, one entry per aggregate. Each entry names the tree it describes, so a figure that has fallen behind the branch says so in the rendered table instead of relying on someone remembering. `file` is a perf/scripts/compare_screen.py output under perf/baselines/; `figures` is for an aggregate that is not screen output.
_stock_comment: The commit the stock arm of every aggregate here was measured against. verify_report.py asserts the ref still resolves to it: if next moves, the figures describe a tree that no longer exists and want re-measuring, which should fail a check rather than be noticed by someone eventually.

aggregates.coverage: 57 scenarios on both arms, all 200 bar the deliberate 404 control; Tier 2 timed 57 of 57 on every leg
aggregates.label: Read loop, 57 scenarios
aggregates.note:
median of five alternating rounds per arm with the arm ORDER reversed on even rounds, both arms proved distinct by content hash -- stock `bd8aafed98d5`, branch `3f21387074b8` -- and each hash reproduced on every arm of every round. Query counts were bit-identical across both deterministic rounds on both arms (3,619 and 897): zero unstable counts in any run, and Tier 2 timed 57 of 57 endpoints on all ten legs.

**Wall clock is the median of each scenario across the five rounds, then summed** -- not the median of the five round totals. Summing rounds first lets the single largest endpoint drive the result, and `api.interface.depth1` is large enough to do it.

Dispersion across rounds is **0.04% on stock and 0.10% on branch**, as the interquartile range of the round totals against their median; max-min is 0.33% and 0.50%. **Per scenario the median scenario's relative standard deviation across rounds is 0.79% on stock and 0.97% on branch.** The totals remain the figure to quote: they are stable because 57 scenarios' errors cancel, so this cumulative number carries weight that an individual per-endpoint wall-clock figure taken from it does not.

**Measured 2026-10-05 against `next` at dc0c3ae99**, after both perf branches were rebased onto it, 38 commits on from 0735993cc. Both arms reproduced their previous query counts exactly -- 3,619 and 897 -- across those 38 commits, which include a major-version dependency update; the measurement host's image was rebuilt from the new lockfile before either arm ran. Summed wall clock moved +0.16% on stock and +0.35% on branch against the 0735993cc run.

The deterministic instruments and the over-HTTP leg ran in one session this time, with the snapshot restored first and the demo stacks stopped for the run, as they were for the previous one.

The scenario set is hand-picked and largely what this branch optimised, so it describes these pages fairly rather than predicting an arbitrary one; the read screen row is the unbiased check

aggregates.label: Read screen, every REST read endpoint
aggregates.note:
median of three alternating rounds per arm with the arm ORDER reversed between rounds, enumerated from the URL resolver at run time rather than from a scenario list, and matched on `(id, kind)` -- the kinds make 518 measurements, and keying on id alone collapses them to 166 and silently changes every total. Arms proved distinct by content hash on every swap.

**Direction, not just the net: 51 measurements improved, 334 unchanged, 133 worse.** The 133 are finding 62's trade made visible -- a prefetch replacing a JOIN is more round trips, each cheaper -- and that finding's own note says the query counter reads it as a regression and must not be the gate. They cost 248 queries against 10,367 saved, 2.4%, and the same rounds put database time down 41.75%.

The stock arm reads 15,041 queries where the 0735993cc run read 15,042. perf/scripts/README.md records the stock arm of this screen jittering by one query on `list.depth1` endpoints between rounds, and that is the size of this difference; it was not traced further.

This row exists to check whether the read loop's result generalises beyond the 57 scenarios this branch optimised. It is REST-only -- no UI page appears in it -- and it is a screening instrument read as a ranked list, not a gate

aggregates.label: Write screen, every POST endpoint
aggregates.note:
median of three alternating rounds per arm, matched on `(id, kind)` rather than id alone -- the three kinds make 259 measurements from 107 endpoints, and keying on id alone collapses them. Arms proved distinct by content hash on every swap.

180 measurements improved, 66 unchanged, 10 worse. **Queries and wall clock come apart on the write path and both belong here**: -17.0% queries against -30.8% wall. Gating on queries alone undervalues the write-path work by roughly 1.8x, because those wins are Python -- serializer reuse, natural-key memoization, a tag cache -- rather than SQL.

All 10 that got worse are `update.x1`, and they cost +20 queries against 3,489 saved. Nine of them are nonetheless faster on wall clock; `ipam-api:vlan-list` is the tenth, flat at +0.09% wall for +2 queries. `extras-api:exporttemplate-list`, which the 0735993cc run found worse on both counts, is 10.7% faster here at the same +1 query -- consistent with that earlier +11.4% having been noise on a three-round median, though nothing here proves it.

Two measurements are new since the 0735993cc run: `create.x1` on `vpn-api:vpnprofilephase1policyassignment-list` and `vpn-api:vpnprofilephase2policyassignment-list`, 22 -> 20 queries each. Both endpoints exist at both bases; why the earlier enumeration did not record them is not established

aggregates.coverage: 11,572 objects created per arm, across 68 models
aggregates.label: Whole-workflow apply, 11,572 objects
aggregates.note:
**the whole-workflow figure: one `databot apply` per arm, creating 11,572 objects across 68 models, two alternating rounds per arm in the order stock/branch/branch/stock, median.** The database is dropped and recreated from an empty template before every arm, so each run builds the dataset from nothing.

The client runs on a second host, not on the box under measurement: it builds every payload itself and is a sustained CPU load, and the perf overlay commits all eight of the measurement host's threads. Measured cost of moving it off-box is +0.16ms per TCP connect against ~198ms average per request.

Wall clock is tight across rounds -- stock 1841/1849s, branch 1042/1040s, spans of 0.43% and 0.19% -- and row counts were identical on all four arms (536 devices, 1,616 interfaces, 1,648 cables), which is what says each arm applied the same work. Query counts come from `pg_stat_statements` reset per arm, so they cover the whole run rather than one request.

The dataset file defines 11,578 objects and databot reports creating 11,572; the six-object difference was not chased, and the figures here describe what was created. The figures are computed from the run's own result lines by `perf/scripts/compare_apply.py`, so verify_report.py recomputes this row like any other.

Two rounds per arm, the four arms the overnight-refresh sequence in perf/scripts/README.md specifies. Measured 2026-10-05 against `next` at dc0c3ae99; the 0735993cc run read 1,836s -> 1,038s and 805,149 -> 635,156 queries
